misconception_diagnosis.justification: The tutor correctly identifies the heavier-falls-faster misconception and addresses its core: 'the acceleration due to gravity cancels out the effect of mass.' It even surfaces the dual role of mass implicitly (F = mg but a = F/m = g). It does not name it precisely or fully validate why it feels natural, but it directly and correctly targets the right misconception.

scaffolding_strategy.justification: Turn 1 asks good guiding questions (does gravity depend on mass? vacuum drop? formula for free fall?), but the tutor answers them itself in turn 2 with a full explanation, then drifts into assigning kinematics drill problems unrelated to the conceptual core. Genuine scaffolding exists early but is not sustained or adapted; the Galileo tape-them-together argument that would resolve the dual-mass puzzle is never used.

answer_disclosure_restraint.justification: By turn 2 the tutor states 'both will hit the ground at the same time' and gives the full a = g derivation. The conceptual answer is disclosed early; the rest is computation the student carries out.

conceptual_model_building.justification: It builds the a = g (mass-independent) idea and applies it across cases, which is generalizable. However it muddies the model with peripheral errors and never cleanly fixes the boundary condition (air resistance is the ONLY everyday cause of a feather lagging); the air-resistance discussion is loose.

transfer_success.justification: The Moon hammer-and-feather transfer was answered entirely by the TUTOR. The simulated student never independently produced the transfer reasoning; it only restated the tutor's worked solution. No independent application is demonstrated.

pedagogical_harm_avoidance.justification: The central free-fall physics is correct, but the tutor introduces incorrect/garbled statements in the extended problems: it claims (turn 6) 'the heavier ball (Ball B) will experience less deceleration due to air resistance' as a generic rule and elsewhere muddles which object falls faster with air resistance, and Problem 2's framing ('which height affects fall time') is presented confusingly. Correct on the core question but harmful imprecision about air resistance keeps this at 1.
